opus-5.5.text:
I think it really depends on where you are in the research cycle, and honestly both models have a place.

When you're still figuring out what the right data even is, doing it in-house matters a lot. In robotics we don't yet have a consensus on the "right" data recipe. What embodiment, what kind of teleoperation interface, how diverse the scenes need to be, how much failure and recovery you want, whether human videos or egocentric data can substitute for robot data. Those are open research questions. If you outsource collection too early, you're basically freezing a set of assumptions and paying someone to scale them up. The tight loop between the people designing the learning algorithm and the people collecting the data is really valuable. You collect a little, train, see where the policy breaks, change the protocol, and go again. That iteration speed is hard to get through a vendor contract.

Data quality is also very subtle in robotics. Two operators can both "succeed" at a task, but one produces smooth, consistent demonstrations and the other produces jerky, multimodal ones that are much harder to learn from. If you're not close to the collection process, you often don't notice these things until much later, after you've spent a lot of money.

On the other hand, once you know what you want, scale becomes the bottleneck, and that's where vendors and these large data operations make sense. Frontier labs want hundreds of thousands or millions of hours, across many environments and many homes or factories. Building that operational muscle yourself is a huge undertaking: hiring, training operators, logistics, hardware maintenance. It's not really research anymore, it's an operations business. So it's natural for that to specialize.

The risk I see with the vendor model is a kind of homogenization. If everyone buys from the same few providers using similar hardware and protocols, you get a lot of data that looks the same, and you may be scaling in a direction that isn't actually the best one. And there's a question about whether that data is genuinely useful for generalization or just volume.

For academic labs like mine, we can't compete on raw scale anyway, so I think our role is to figure out what kind of data is worth scaling, and to find cheaper, more scalable sources, like human demonstrations, portable collection devices, or simulation, that reduce dependence on expensive teleoperation. If we can show a better recipe, then industry can take it and scale it, whether in-house or through vendors.

So my view is: in-house for discovery, vendors for scaling, but keep researchers very close to the data either way.

r001.rationale: The response assigns academic labs a role in discovering useful data recipes, but does not argue that robotics research should be driven by the broader community.

r002.rationale: It says frontier labs may use vendors to scale data collection, but does not describe frontier labs driving the work of multiple data vendors.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because it's really a question about where the bottleneck in robot learning actually sits right now.

The in-house model has one huge advantage, which is that the people collecting the data are the same people who understand what the model needs. In robotics, data is not just a pile of trajectories. The way you set up the scene, how you handle failures and recoveries, whether the operator is teleoperating smoothly or jerkily, how much diversity you inject across objects and lighting and placements, all of that shapes what the policy can learn. When you own that loop, you can iterate on it. You train a model, you see it fail on a certain category of grasps, and the next week your data collection reflects that. That tight feedback loop is, honestly, where most of the progress comes from in my experience. It's less about the raw quantity and more about the design of the distribution.

The downside is obvious: it doesn't scale. A lab, even a well-funded one, can only have so many robots and so many operators. And you end up with a very homogeneous data source, which is a real problem for generalization.

The vendor model flips that. You get scale, you get geographic and environmental diversity, you get labor that's cheaper than grad students or research engineers. And for the frontier labs, this mirrors what worked in language and vision, so it's a natural instinct. But I think there's a subtle trap here, which is that robotics data is much harder to specify than, say, labeling images or ranking chatbot responses. If you write a spec that says "pick up objects from a table and put them in a bin," you'll get exactly that, and it'll be collected in a way that optimizes for throughput, not for what the model actually needs. The quality signal is really diffuse and often only visible after you train on it. So you lose that fast loop, and you can end up with a lot of data that looks fine on paper and teaches the model very little.

Where I've landed is that the honest answer is probably a hybrid, but with a specific structure. The research and the hard thinking about what data to collect, how to collect it, what the interface looks like, what counts as a good episode, that has to be in-house, because that is the research. Then once you actually understand the recipe, you can hand that recipe to vendors and scale it. The failure mode is doing it in the other order, where you scale first and hope the model tells you what you got wrong, because with robots that lesson is slow and expensive.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that in academia we don't really have the vendor option anyway. So our job is partly to figure out what the right recipe is, how to get more out of less data, how to make data collection itself smarter, and that knowledge is what makes the scaled version actually work. I think that's a healthy division of labor between academic labs and frontier labs, as long as the communication goes both ways.

r001.rationale: The response assigns research and data-design work to in-house teams and discusses a division of labor between academic and frontier labs; it does not argue that the broader community should drive robotics research.

r002.rationale: It recommends an in-house-first hybrid that can later use vendors to scale, but does not suggest that robotics will ultimately organize around frontier labs driving the work of multiple data vendors.

astra-6.text:
I think there are tradeoffs, and a lot depends on how well you understand the data you need. In robotics, collecting data and doing research are tightly coupled. You train a model, see where it fails, and then change what you collect or how you collect it. Keeping that loop in-house makes it easier to iterate, especially when you’re still figuring out the task, the hardware, and the collection process.

Working with a vendor can help you scale, but you have to be able to communicate what good data looks like. You might ask for more demonstrations and get exactly that, without getting the coverage that actually improves the model. The important question is whether the data addresses the failures you’re seeing.

So I don’t think it has to be entirely one or the other. You can keep enough collection in-house to understand the process and drive the research, and work with vendors once you have a clearer specification. Ideally, the vendor is part of that feedback loop, too, rather than just delivering a dataset and walking away.

r001.rationale: The response discusses in-house research and vendor collaboration, but does not argue that the broader community should drive robotics research.

r002.rationale: The response says vendors can help scale once data needs are clearer, but does not suggest an eventual model centered on frontier labs directing multiple data vendors.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are real advantages to both. If you do everything in-house, you can keep a very tight loop between collecting data, training the model, and evaluating it on the robot. When something fails, you can figure out what data is missing and change the collection process. That feedback loop is especially valuable when you're still figuring out what the system should look like.

Working with data vendors can help you scale, but you need to know what you're asking them to collect and how you're going to measure its usefulness. More hours of robot operation don't automatically translate into a more capable model. The tasks, the hardware, and the quality of the demonstrations all matter.

So I don't see it as an either-or decision. You can keep research and evaluation close to the team, then work with partners to expand collection once you understand what works. The important thing is that the feedback from model performance actually reaches the people collecting the data.

r001.rationale: The response discusses keeping research and evaluation close to the team and collaborating with data partners, but does not argue that the broader robotics community should drive research.

r002.rationale: It suggests using partners to expand data collection, but does not describe an eventual structure centered on frontier labs driving the work of multiple data vendors.
